books.title: Adam Bede
books.author: George Eliot
books.desc: In a farming village of 1799, an honest carpenter, a vain dairymaid, a charming young squire and a Methodist preacher are caught up in love, temptation and conscience.
about: In the rural community of Hayslope in 1799, Adam Bede is a skilled and upright carpenter, respected by everyone. He loves Hetty Sorrel, the pretty and vain young niece of the farmer Martin Poyser, but Hetty dreams of a grander life and is flattered by the attentions of Arthur Donnithorne, the good-natured young heir to the local estate. Hetty's cousin Dinah Morris, a gentle Methodist preacher, watches over the village with quiet compassion.

Eliot portrays country life, its work, speech and humour, with close and affectionate detail, and gives as much dignity to farmers and craftsmen as to the gentry. The novel explores moral responsibility, the consequences of small choices, suffering and forgiveness, and it shows the realism and sympathy for ordinary people that mark all her fiction.

Adam Bede was George Eliot's first full-length novel, published in 1859 by John Blackwood. Its success established the reputation of the author, whose real name was Mary Ann Evans, and it remains one of her best-loved works.

books.title: Jude the Obscure
books.author: Thomas Hardy
books.desc: A poor village stonemason dreams of studying at the great university city of Christminster, but class, marriage and society stand in his way.
about: Jude Fawley, a poor orphan raised by his great-aunt in a Wessex village, longs to become a scholar at Christminster, the university city whose towers he can glimpse from afar. Teaching himself Latin and Greek while working as a stonemason, he is drawn into an early marriage with Arabella Donn, a lively country girl, and later meets his cousin Sue Bridehead, a bright, independent and unconventional young woman.

Hardy writes a bleak and searching novel about thwarted ambition, the barriers of class and education, and the rules that church and society placed on marriage. Jude and Sue question the conventions of their time, and Hardy follows their struggles with deep sympathy and without easy consolation.

The novel was first serialised in Harper's New Monthly Magazine from December 1894 to November 1895, in a cut version, and published in book form in 1895. Its frank treatment of sex, marriage and religion caused an outcry among many reviewers and readers. It was Hardy's last novel; Christminster is his fictional version of Oxford.

books.title: Little Dorrit
books.author: Charles Dickens
books.desc: Born inside a London debtors' prison, gentle Amy Dorrit cares for her proud father, while Arthur Clennam, home after twenty years abroad, senses a family secret.
about: Amy Dorrit, known as Little Dorrit, was born and raised in the Marshalsea, the debtors' prison in London where her father William Dorrit has lived for so long that he is called its Father. She works quietly to support her family. Arthur Clennam returns to London after twenty years abroad and, suspecting that his cold and severe mother owes some wrong to the Dorrits, sets out to help them, coming up against the bureaucracy of the Circumlocution Office.

Dickens builds the novel around the image of imprisonment, real and figurative: debt, pride, social ambition, guilt and the endless red tape of government. He satirises officialdom and financial speculation while drawing a moving portrait of goodness in Little Dorrit herself and a vast cast of comic and sinister characters.

Little Dorrit was published in monthly parts from December 1855 to June 1857, with illustrations by Hablot Knight Browne ("Phiz"). Dickens's own father had been imprisoned for debt in the Marshalsea in 1824. The serial was a great success on first publication.

books.title: Agnes Grey
books.author: Anne Brontë
books.desc: A young clergyman's daughter becomes a governess to help her family, and finds that the homes of the wealthy can be harder places than she imagined.
about: Agnes Grey, the younger daughter of a poor clergyman, decides to earn her own living as a governess to help her family. Her first post, with the Bloomfield family, brings her unruly, spoiled children and parents who give her responsibility without authority. In her second place, with the wealthy Murrays, she must look after self-centred young ladies, and her only comforts are the countryside, her own faith and the company of the kind local curate, Mr Weston.

Told in Agnes's own calm and honest voice, the novel gives a clear-eyed picture of the isolation and humiliations a governess could face, and of how the rich treated those who worked for them. Anne Brontë writes plainly and with quiet irony, and the book is a story of integrity, patience and modest hope.

Agnes Grey was Anne Brontë's first novel, drawn closely on her own years as a governess. It was published in December 1847 by Thomas Cautley Newby under the pen name Acton Bell, in the same set of volumes as her sister Emily's Wuthering Heights.
books.author_short: English novelist and poet (1820–1849), the youngest of the Brontë sisters, author of Agnes Grey and The Tenant of Wildfell Hall.
author_long: Anne Brontë was born on 17 January 1820 at Thornton, Yorkshire, the youngest of the six children of the Reverend Patrick Brontë and his wife Maria Branwell, and grew up at Haworth with her sisters Charlotte and Emily and her brother Branwell. She worked as a governess for several years, including from 1840 at Thorp Green, a country house near York, in the family of the Reverend Edmund Robinson. She died, probably of tuberculosis, at Scarborough on 28 May 1849, aged 29.

Writing as Acton Bell, she published poems with her sisters in 1846, then Agnes Grey in 1847, based on her experience as a governess. Her second and last novel, The Tenant of Wildfell Hall (1848), a bold story of a woman leaving an abusive marriage, is often described as one of the first feminist novels.

books.title: Rob Roy
books.author: Walter Scott
books.desc: A young Englishman follows a treacherous cousin into the Scottish Highlands on the eve of the 1715 Jacobite rising, and crosses paths with the outlaw Rob Roy MacGregor.
about: Frank Osbaldistone, the son of a London merchant, refuses to join his father's business and is sent to stay with his uncle's rough, hunting family in Northumberland. There he meets the clever, spirited Diana Vernon and his scheming cousin Rashleigh. When Rashleigh makes off with documents vital to the honour and fortune of Frank's father, Frank follows him north into Scotland and the Highlands, where he meets the Glasgow merchant Bailie Nicol Jarvie and the legendary outlaw Rob Roy MacGregor.

Scott sets a story of adventure, rivalry and romance against the political and economic background of the Jacobite rising of 1715. He contrasts commercial Lowland Scotland with the old clan society of the Highlands, and mixes vivid landscapes, Scots dialogue and humour with a sympathetic portrait of a world about to disappear.

Rob Roy was published in 1817 as one of the Waverley novels, which Scott issued anonymously. It was hugely popular and was soon adapted for the stage. The French translation offered here is by Auguste-Jean-Baptiste Defauconpret, published in 1830.
